I'll do some performance analysis on both approaches and see if there is any benefit here. I'm also happy to explore specialization constants to see if they make a difference.

As I understand it, the old code would start executing all three branches at the same time before determining which to continue with. The new code would start executing two branches at the same time and might figure out which to continue with before reaching the next branch. (Making the SDR branch less likely to saturate the available ALUs).

But I might be entirely wrong, so please just ignore my comments on the performance of this. It’s best to not bother changing this for the purpose of optimizing.

That said, my suggestion fixes a logic issue (both HDR formats should have identical clamping with the same code comment text; the current PR has different clamping/clipping with different code comment explanations), reduces duplicated code, improves some comments, and makes the code a bit more readable in understanding what the differences are between the two HDR formats. So please consider applying the suggestion for reasons entirely unrelated to hypothetical performance.

Drive-by comments (I work on AOSP graphics/display and saw this shared out):

1. Generally android devices don't support fp16 as an output/scanout format. Often, fp16 is blit to rgba8888 under the hood on the gpu to compensate which is bad for power, and a lot of display panels are 8-bit anyways. You might be able to use OverlayProperties (https://developer.android.com/reference/android/hardware/OverlayProperties#isCombinationSupported(int,%20int)) to discover this, or you could unconditionally just try to use RGBA8888 instead.
2. Most devices (not just Android) do an undefined tonemapping to display conditions for HDR10. So while it's great that you're querying the HDR/SDR ratio to figure out an SDR white level in your signal, the downstream tonemapping will probably shift your white level. I think this is hard to solve (more details below), so this is more of an fyi.

The view system solves these problems by rendering to 8-bit Display P3, and setting extended range brightness on our compositor apis (https://developer.android.com/ndk/reference/group/native-activity#asurfacetransaction_setextendedrangebrightness), which both set the current SDR white level and "vote" for a desired hdr headroom that the app wants. The app then treats 1.0 == display max, and color manages SDR white to the appropriate level inside of its content. The compositor then maps the app's SDR white to the system SDR white to try to keep them consistent.

So that way the view system hits a power-efficient display path on all devices, and tonemapping is essentially source-based. But, particularly the extended range brightness part, requires fairly deep integration with our SurfaceControl apis.

in addition to registering for the hdr/sdr ratio, you might want to consider voting for an upper-bound with an api like https://developer.android.com/reference/android/view/SurfaceView#setDesiredHdrHeadroom(float), either as an engine-default or letting the game configure it (probably, not all games need or want an 8x headroom that some devices are able to achieve)

two comments out of curiosity here:

* generally i'm curious if you'd find min and avg luminance useful at all. e.g. right now you're only using max luminance to figure out your reference SDR white (my general hunch is actually that they're not very useful :))
* generally i'm curious if you find max luminance outside of figuring out reference SDR white. In low light conditions, many devices' auto-brightness features will set display luminance to single-digit nits, so my general hunch is also that max luminance isn't very useful for tonemapping either since there's no information about the viewing environment.

if you don't need a meaningful alpha channel RGBA1010102 support is pretty broad, and that'll give you 10-bits of color which is good enough in all honesty (most panels are 8-bit, and virtually no panels are more than 10-bits)

Thanks for looking at and commenting on this PR, AMouri! Your feedback is very helpful!

> Most devices (not just Android) do an undefined tonemapping to display conditions for HDR10. So while it's great that you're querying the HDR/SDR ratio to figure out an SDR white level in your signal, the downstream tonemapping will probably shift your white level. I think this is hard to solve (more details below), so this is more of an fyi.

This is a major issue for for game developers: if there's any way to circumvent any downstream tonemapping, this is what we want to do. On Apple devices, this [is trivial and we've had good success](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/106814).

On Windows, Mac OS, iOS, and Wayland (Linux) Godot requests the reference white luminance (a.k.a. SDR white level) of the system and matches that. This way, Godot games will always appear as bright in HDR mode as the rest of the host operating system or other SDR games. On these platforms, we request the current maximum luminance and either poll or subscribe to events for when this changes. Our engine's tonemappers respond to the available HDR headroom and adapt the rendered image to "fit" within the available range.

The process you described where the app "votes" for a desired HDR headroom sounds strange to me. I understand this is a very desirable behaviour for HDR video, and may be the only way that HDR video could work... but for a game engine that can adapt to the available range, I don't know how we could reasonably work with this.

Do you have any further suggestions or details on how to do the following?
- Avoid downstream tonemapping behaviour
- Determine available HDR headroom based on current display brightness
- Match SDR reference white luminance

(Specifically, achieve this without needing to vote on a desired HDR headroom?)

Godot's tonemapping is intentionally quite simple; there is nowhere we would make use of a minimum luminance, average luminance, or full screen max luminance.

Viewing environment is obviously hugely important for HDR. In its simplest form, darker Godot games will be easy to make with the "extended dynamic range" paradigm that we're using: values above reference white luminance (above `1.0`) will be limited to highlights and therefore a very small portion of the screen.

For games that have scenes with a large portion of the screen being above reference white luminance, things get more complicated: in this case, the human eye may adapt to these bright values being a new "reference white luminance" or the player may find this to be uncomfortably bright and not respecting their device brightness setting. For these cases, we put the onus on the game developer to limit their scene values for these specific scenes, such as limiting to an HDR headroom up to `1.5` of reference white lumiance, for example. Because this is scene-specific, this is not something we can do automatically within the Godot game engine.

(Note to others reading this: the game developer can limit their scene values easily when not using tonemapping, but when using tonemapping, we will need to add an "output range limit" parameter, which [I will make a PR for in the future](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/13749) when I've settled on the exact design and also when I have time.)

> if there's any way to circumvent any downstream tonemapping, this is what we want to do

that's part of the extended range brightness api i mentioned above. if this api is used in conjunction with a buffer that is encoded with an sRGB transfer, then you can specify an HDR signal that is guaranteed not to tonemap downstream. It's how the view system is able to support HDR images, for example.

> The process you described where the app "votes" for a desired HDR headroom sounds strange to me. I understand this is a very desirable behaviour for HDR video, and may be the only way that HDR video could work... but for a game engine that can adapt to the available range, I don't know how we could reasonably work with this.

You can just request the range that you would be using in your scene. I'm sure you have some guardrails, like you probably don't expect a 10k nit panel to have an SDR white level of 10 nits.

But regardless, you could vote for a very large headroom, and the system will clamp it to the maximum that it can support. (and, the reason for *why* you need to vote for a headroom is if there's no HDR content the screen will control its max luminance to only have a headroom of 1. So you need to tell the screen that your sRGB signal is actually HDR, so that the screen can actually ramp up in brightness to allow for headroom, while keeping SDR white fixed).

I understand this to be the sort of thing that could be changed at runtime for the specific purpose of power saving.

So this could be implemented as a project setting for Android that limits HDR headroom for the purpose of power saving and could be changed at runtime to give power savings for bright scenes on phones with OLED screens, for example. I believe this power saving option would be suitable for implementation as a followup PR, to reduce the complexity and effort required to get this first version of HDR output implemented.

Importantly, when it is implemented, changes to the desired headroom would need to feed back to the maximum luminance values that we get from the host system.

Got it. it also sounds like Godot's rendering model is relative (1.0 == SDR white, rather than 1.0 == 80 nits or 100 nits or 203 nits or XXX nits happens to be what people feel ought to be the SDR reference white level).

Headroom implicitly encodes the viewing environment fwiw. At least on androd, it's not uncommon for a device's headroom to be nearly 1.0 in bright conditions (so that SDR can compete with the sun), while very large in darker viewing environments (so that HDR can look its best).

The vote is just to indicate to the system how much brighter it should try to drive the panel, and thus how much additional power to spend. You can get away with just treating it like a boolean if you don't want to think much about it, if "use hdr" is false just go back to requesting the default of 1.0 headroom (aka, no HDR), and if true request some hardcoded constant, like 8.0 (not unlike the EDR limit on iPhone)

The View system actually defaults to a requested amount of 5.0 when HDR is enabled because that's where we found banding to start being significant with RGBA_8888 (and we need the alpha and thus cannot use 1010102), but that was in pure gradients as is typical with UIs. https://cs.android.com/android/platform/superproject/main/+/main:frameworks/base/libs/hwui/Properties.cpp;drc=61197364367c9e404c7da6900658f1b16c42d0da;l=111

Regardless of the amount you request, the amount you _get_ is determined by the system via a variety of policies and hardware limitations, so you need to react to https://developer.android.com/reference/android/view/Display#getHdrSdrRatio() & https://developer.android.com/reference/android/view/Display#registerHdrSdrRatioChangedListener(java.util.concurrent.Executor,%20java.util.function.Consumer%3Candroid.view.Display%3E) to adjust dynamically to the system constraints.

So if you just always vote for some maximum value, like 8, then the rest should end up feeling very "EDR-like". The benefit of the voting system is it lets the system get away with less power in cases where not much HDR is desired, which is especially prevalent in mixed SDR/HDR scenarios like photo thumbnails in text messages. See for example the "constrainedHigh" option on other platforms. The desiredRatio is essentially that, but more flexible. And you may want to even intentionally use a low value, like just 2-4, so that more of your available bits are for the SDR range that makes up the majority of the scene and there's less total power cost to the feature, given this is running on a battery almost always

Yes! Looks like we're on the same page. Thanks for reading through and responding to my comments.

Thanks for the detailed comments; this is all very timely and helpful before we merge the first version of HDR output support on Android.

Internally, we use F16 buffers for all HDR rendering in Godot. There was a lot of discussion about this, but non-HDR rendering is still well supported with 8 bit or 10 bit formats, so it's a tradeoff the game developer will need to make for their game.

It sounds like, for HDR output on Android, it might be best to:

1. take our linear F16 values and encode them (unclamped) using the nonlinear sRGB tranfser function
2. write the result to a `RGBA1010102` buffer
3. use the View system with a user-configurable "Android HDR headroom" that defaults to something between `10.0` and `100.0`, but can be reduced by the developer to improve power efficiency or reduce banding

It's good to know that an 8 bit nonlinear sRGB-encoded buffer shouldn't be pushed past `5.0`. To be honest, I would have expected a fair bit lower. I don't have experience with 10 bit buffers that have been coded with the nonlinear sRGB transfer function, so I really don't know where banding might start to be visible, but I expect that there probably can be a fair bit of headroom, even up to something like `30.0` or `40.0` (but probably not `100.0`, given that this is somewhat like the ratio used in a PQ-encoded signal, which does show minor banding with a 10 bit buffer even with the better transfer function.)
Apple '26 OSs introduced a similar API to limit the headroom to reduce maximum brightness

Hmm, good to know! Maybe adding an all-platform HDR limit parameter in Godot 4.8 might make sense. This would feed into Android and iOS functions for power saving, and also simply tonemap/clip to the lower value when the available is higher. Originally, I was hesitant about the lack of flexibility with this approach, but now that I see its linked to power saving options on Android and iOS, it might be the best approach.
dithering techniques do a lot of heavy lifting for making sRGB gradients with a high headroom still look good
Yes, we have a fairly effective dither "debanding" we have built into the engine. We'll make sure that's available for Android's HDR path.

Note that if you go this route, which we know using the ASurfaceControl APIs for this is not the most friendly thing and want to make easier at some point, then you actually need to use a _scaled_ sRGB transfer function by the current hdrSdrRatio, which is what you then tell the system you used via the "currentBufferRatio" parameter.  An example of this using what's essentially an ICC parametric curve type 4 can be found here: https://cs.android.com/android/platform/superproject/main/+/main:frameworks/base/libs/hwui/utils/Color.cpp;drc=61197364367c9e404c7da6900658f1b16c42d0da;l=418

This is because the 8/10-bit values span the range of 0 to currentHdrSdrRatio rather than 0 to SDR as it would in a normal sRGB buffer.

> It's good to know that an 8 bit nonlinear sRGB-encoded buffer shouldn't be pushed past 5.0. To be honest, I would have expected a fair bit lower. 

If it helps remember that you are rendering directly to the current display range, and the display itself is physically typically gamma 2.2. So all of those fancy HDR10(+)/whatever PQ signals end up getting shoved out of an 8-bit gamma2.2 panel at the end of the day regardless :)

If you are using a 1010102 buffer you'll still have temporal dithering to help, but if you're using 8888 then you won't really. The View system forces spatial dithering on all content to significantly help here, but if you're using 1010102 then you'll get the hardware spatial dithering in addition to temporal dithering and so it should be strictly better than any PQ signal as you aren't wasting bits on range that isn't used.

re. headroom limits i would also just note, in-line with the power discussions, is that a high headroom is not necessarily what a game or users would want, either, even if there's no visible banding.

like when headroom is very high, white SDR assets become perceptually grey (there's a simulated image in https://android-developers.googleblog.com/2025/09/hdr-and-user-interfaces.html demonstrating this). it's fine to give developers control if they really want a high headroom, but it's probably something to note as design guidance.

Ah, yes, the points about the display hardware all make sense to me. It's good to know that some dithering is being applied, but since this will be applied after we've already quantized to an 8/10 bit buffer, I expect this dithering will not be as effective as what we're able to do with our floating point values just before we quantize to our integer frame buffer...

> This is because the 8/10-bit values span the range of 0 to currentHdrSdrRatio rather than 0 to SDR as it would in a normal sRGB buffer.

Sounds like this should be as simple as scaling our linear floating point values (where 1.0 matches SDR white) by `currentBufferRatio` to get a value in the range of `[0.0, currentBufferRatio]`. Then apply the nonlinear sRGB transfer function and write to the 8 or 10 bit integer buffer. Not too crazy, just an "unconventional" usage of sRGB. This is basically the exact same thing that we currently do in this PR with the PQ transfer function. This can be seen in the changes to `blit.glsl` of this PR.

> it's fine to give developers control if they really want a high headroom, but it's probably something to note as design guidance.

Yep, this will likely come in Godot 4.8 when we have a good API for this. Sounds like it will probably be a property of the `Window` class: `hdr_headroom_limit` that will be `-1.0` (unlimited) by default on most platforms and `20.0` (give or take ~10) by default on platforms like Android that have this as a first-class feature with power saving and precision benefits.

For this PR we can probably hardcode the limit until we expose this property in a later Godot version.

If we use the view system, it sounds like the buffer might be [expected to be Display P3](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/101977#discussion_r2822542014). If this is the case and there's no way to simply tell the destination that it should be Rec. 709/sRGB primaries and we need to convert from Rec. 709 primaries to Display P3 primaries, here's the matrix:

```
const mat3 rec709_to_p3 = mat3(
	0.822461968714362, 0.033194198850962, 0.017082630721120,
	0.177538031285638, 0.966805801149038, 0.072397440663963,
	0.000000000000000, 0.000000000000000, 0.910519928614917);
```

Source: https://www.colour-science.org:8010/apps/rgb_colourspace_transformation_matrix

"view system" in that comment means specifically Android Views, like ImageView, Button, TextView, etc...   and the choices of the 2D renderer behind it. Godot is not part of that world since it's doing its own rendering and has its own output. So you can do Display P3 or Rec 709/sRGB or BT2020 or whatever gamut you want, you aren't required to match anything else necessarily.  Older / lower end devices could only handle a single display-wide gamut, so anything else would be GPU composited first. But newer ones can handle multiple color gamuts in hardware just fine, there's now an OverlayProperties API that will tell you this: https://developer.android.com/reference/android/hardware/OverlayProperties?hl=en#isMixedColorSpacesSupported()

But if you just want to always be in Rec 709 while still taking advantage of extendedRangeBrightness, that's perfectly valid. You just need to ensure you tell the system what you did with eg https://developer.android.com/ndk/reference/group/native-activity#asurfacetransaction_setbufferdataspace (note that standard, range, and transfer are all independent enums that you can freely combine, this is more obvious with the SDK-equivalent: https://developer.android.com/reference/android/hardware/DataSpace#pack(int,%20int,%20int)
Thanks for the clarification!

I don’t have any documentation :(

Since downstream monitor tonemapping for HDR10 is so wildly undefined it’s hard to say what happens for sure re. HDR/SDR ratio or SDR white level inside of the signal. There’s just no spec suggesting what a monitor should do.

As a general rule you might be able to assume:

* if you send an HDR10 signal whose content and metadata exceed the monitor capabilities, then the content will either be clipped or compressed in some way.
* If you send an HDR10 signal whose content and metadata fit within the monitor capabilities, then the content *might* not be tonemapped at all

but unfortunately that’s all a lot of hope

Btw the video industry recognizes this is a huge problem too since no one can trust that their hdr content can be faithfully reproduced, so SMPTE is working through yet another standard: https://github.com/SMPTE/st2094-50, which is backed by a lot of industry players
So long term that might help, depending on how 2094-50 shakes out + makes it’s way through displayport, hdmi, or other standards

Thanks for all of the information.

What I've done for now is switch to using the A2R10G10B10 format for the swap chain which appears to have improved the contrast issues I was seeing on my Google Fold. Things look reasonable on that device now.

I'm not sure if we should implement a max headroom now or follow up with another PR. I understand there are power saving and other benefits to configuring one, though I'm not getting a sense of how critical that is for games that tend to be battery hungry already. 

The tricky bit for games is we often don't know how bright a scene may be, since the underlying lighting may be modeled after realistic units. So, we are forced into a tradeoff between reproducing the scene as faithfully as we can using the display we have, or imposing a cap that may save some power but fails to utilize the full capability of the display.

I strongly feel that for 4.7 the Android Android "desired HDR headroom" should be hardcoded to something like `8.0` (this is the highest that my Google Pixel is able to go and also the highest my iPhone 13 Pro is able to go, so this makes sense as a good number to hardcode) and not exposed to the user in any way.

Godot 4.8 will introduce a new `Window.output_linear_value_limit` property which will be available on all platforms. For most platforms it will probably be best to default to `128.0` (for reasons I will describe in my upcoming proposal) and for Android and iOS it will probably be best to default to `8.0`.

In 4.8, this new property may be linked directly to the Android "desired HDR headroom" and equivalent on iOS.

I am focused on finishing 4.7 for now, but once that's wrapped up, I will start work on the user-facing `Window.output_linear_value_limit` property and all of the related platform-specific features.
